1: Manufacturing is steadily pushing ahead with automation and intelligent transformation, and the shop floor now demands more from equipment operation management and anomaly response. Getting agent technology more deeply involved in routine inspection and anomaly handling has become an important direction for improving production and operations efficiency.
2: In production operations, stable line operation depends on routine inspection and anomaly handling. On-site staff must judge problems from equipment status and production information and coordinate the follow-up. Some lines, for example, still need a manual restart after power is restored, and a slow response extends downtime and hurts production. Reducing repetitive work and speeding up anomaly response is therefore a practical need in line operations.
3: Agents offer a new way to do this kind of work: combining business information with tool calls to support the whole flow from spotting a problem to carrying out the fix. In such scenarios the agent can analyse the cause of a stoppage (a power cut, say) from operating documents and the equipment's current state, and once the conditions for running are confirmed, call the right tool to bring the line back. Take the case where the conveyor belt is still not running after power is restored, and compare how a person and an agent handle it:
4: Building such an agent by hand, however, takes a lot of effort: you still have to write the frontend and backend code and tune the results. Fortunately Penguin Harness is a framework for automatically developing and optimising agents, and it can greatly cut the manual work involved. The user provides the business requirements, example inputs, format specifications and MCP tools; Penguin Harness develops the agent and its companion web app accordingly, and keeps improving the agent's task performance with evaluation feedback. 57: README.md is the task document handed to Penguin Harness; it explains what this development task is and how to go about it. Here is a brief summary of its content:
58: contracts/ defines the format specifications for input data, equipment status, operations and reports. For example, which fields the input data must contain and what structure the analysis report should follow are agreed here.

60: For example, events.jsonl records the equipment status change log. From the two log lines excerpted below you can see the equipment lost power, and after power was restored the drive was ready but still had to wait for a new run permission before it would start.
61: These logs are handed to the agent together with the operating data and workstation images, for it to analyse the cause of the stoppage and the conditions for recovery.
62: evaluation/ is used for the evaluation and optimisation after development; we cover it in chapter 4.
64: Besides reading the existing business materials, the agent application also needs to query the equipment's current status and perform the right operations on it.
65: In this example we want the agent application to complete two tasks: restoring the conveyor belt and switching on the cooling fan. So interfaces/ provides the two corresponding MCP services. Each service exposes the relevant MCP tools for the agent to query equipment status and perform operations. The two MCP services are for:
68: Query power and conveyor status, and restore conveyor operation once the conditions are met
70: Query temperature and fan status, and switch on the cooling fan
71: With these two MCP services, the agent application can control the equipment and complete the task. For example, if the conveyor is still not running after power is restored, the agent can first check equipment status through power-control and request a belt start once the conditions are met. If the stoppage was caused by overheating, it first switches on the fan through cooling-control, waits for the temperature to drop, then checks whether the belt can start.
72: For the agent to use these two MCP services, Penguin Harness must also integrate them during development. So we put the materials for both MCPs in the workspace (interfaces/) in advance, as a reference for Penguin Harness.
73: Also, in this example both MCP services run in a local simulated environment, and the start-up, cooling and output changes shown later also come from that simulation.
74: Now we know what the two MCPs are for. If you want their more specific configuration, see interfaces/README.md.
